content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Routing for Site-to-Site VPN

Routing for Site-to-Site VPN

Control how traffic leaves your VPC and reaches on-premises networks, and vice versa.

In this lesson
Static routes, route propagation, and troubleshooting.
Coming up
AWS CLI examples and verification steps.
Goal
Confirm bi-directional routing over the VPN.
Virtual Private Gateway
VGW is the AWS next hop for on-prem routes.
Example IDs used in this chapter: VPC vpc-0123456789abcdef0, VGW vgw-0abcdef1234567890
Explore Key Topics
Static Routes
Manual route entries pointing on-premises CIDRs to the VGW; required when not using BGP.
Route Propagation
Enable VGW propagation and allow BGP advertisements to populate the VPC route table automatically.
Troubleshooting
Check routes, security groups, NACLs, tunnel status and BGP state to pinpoint failures.
Visual Concept
Flow
EC2 instance → VPC route table entry → VGW → VPN tunnel → On-premises router
This strip summarizes the next hops you must configure so packets leave AWS and arrive on-premises.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your attention on the practical routing skills needed for a Site-to-Site VPN. First, you will understand how routing behaves in a hybrid cloud setup so you can reason about packet flow and next hops. Second, you will be able to configure VPC route tables to direct traffic toward your Virtual Private Gateway, using either static routes or automated propagation. Third, you will learn to interpret BGP advertisements from the Customer Gateway so you can verify which prefixes are visible to AWS. Finally, you will acquire troubleshooting techniques: checking routes on both sides, verifying security groups and firewalls, and diagnosing common misconfigurations like overlapping CIDRs. Each objective is framed with examples and a short mnemonic to help retention. For instance, think of route propagation as an automatic mail carrier that delivers addresses learned from BGP into your VPC route book. Practically, you’ll run AWS CLI commands to enable propagation and to add static routes, and you’ll practice verifying the resulting entries. The goal is not only to know the steps but to reason about why a route is missing or why traffic is blocked. This chapter rewards careful verification of both routing tables and firewall rules so the network works end-to-end.

screens.title: What routing means in a hybrid cloud
screens.narratorSegment: In a hybrid cloud setup, routing is the set of rules that tell a host where to send packets when the destination is outside its local subnet. On AWS, each subnet points to a route table that lists destination CIDR blocks and the next hop for matching traffic. For Site-to-Site VPNs the next hop is commonly the Virtual Private Gateway. On-premises routers have matching rules that send packets toward the tunnel or a specific inside-tunnel address. The key claim is this: packets only travel where both sides have explicit knowledge of the remote CIDR and a valid next hop. A concrete example from this chapter uses a VPC CIDR of 172.31.0.0/16 and an on-premises CIDR of 10.0.0.0/16. If an EC2 instance with private IP 172.31.10.5 wants to reach 10.0.2.20, its subnet route table must contain a route for 10.0.0.0/16 pointing to the VGW so the packet is forwarded into the tunnel. A common misconception is believing that an active VPN tunnel alone guarantees connectivity. Tunnels only carry packets when the routing tables on both ends direct traffic toward them. The takeaway: always verify both AWS route tables and on-premises routing entries whenever reachability fails. Which side will you check first when you see a failed ping?

keyIdea.text: Routing is mutual: both AWS and on-premises devices must have explicit routes to each other's CIDR blocks with correct next hops.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › What routing means
Definition
Routing determines the next hop for traffic leaving a subnet so packets reach remote CIDRs across the VPN.
Claim
Both sides must have explicit routes for the other side’s CIDR blocks.
Example
VPC 172.31.0.0/16 needs a route to 10.0.0.0/16 with target vgw-0abcdef1234567890 to reach on-premises hosts.
Misconception
An UP VPN tunnel does not imply routing is correct; missing route table entries can still block traffic.
Key Takeaway

Always confirm route entries on AWS and on-premises devices so the VGW has a clear next hop for remote CIDRs.

Annotated Example
Subnet CIDR: 172.31.0.0/16 VPC ID: vpc-0123456789abcdef0 On-prem CIDR: 10.0.0.0/16 VGW: vgw-0abcdef1234567890 If instance 172.31.10.5 → destination 10.0.2.20 Route: 10.0.0.0/16 → target vgw-0abcdef1234567890
Question: If a ping from EC2 to on-prem fails, do you check the AWS route table or the on-prem route first? Try both: a missing route on either side can create one-way or no connectivity.

screens.title: Adding static routes in AWS VPC route tables
screens.narratorSegment: Static routing means you add explicit entries in your VPC route table for each on-premises CIDR and set the target to the Virtual Private Gateway. This process is necessary when you selected static routing at VPN creation or when you need full control over exact prefixes. For example, use the destination 10.0.0.0/16 and set the target to vgw-0abcdef1234567890 so any instance with matching traffic sends packets to the VGW. Important operational advice: every subnet uses an associated route table, so ensure you add the static route to the route table associated with the subnets that require access to on-premises resources. A common mistake is adding a route to the wrong route table or forgetting an association. Another misstep is assuming a single route table is global across the VPC — it is not; associations determine which subnets inherit those routes. The procedural steps are straightforward: open the VPC console, pick the correct route table, and create a route with the on-premises destination and the VGW target. If you use the CLI, run aws ec2 create-route with route-table-id, destination-cidr-block and vpn-gateway-id. Always verify after creation by listing routes and testing connectivity. Closing takeaway: static routes are simple but brittle; they are best for stable, predictable address plans.

keyIdea.title: Static route pattern
keyIdea.text: Add a route for each on-premises CIDR with the VGW as the target and ensure the route table is associated with the correct subnets.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Static Routes
Step-by-step
1
Select the route table associated with subnets needing on-prem access.
2
Create a route: Destination = on-prem CIDR (example 10.0.0.0/16), Target = VGW ID.
3
Verify route existence and association, then test with a ping or application traffic.
CLI example
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id rtb-0fedcba9876543210 \
  --destination-cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16 \
  --vpn-gateway-id vgw-0abcdef1234567890
Key Takeaway

Static routes are explicit and deterministic, but require manual updates and correct route table associations to work.

Common mistakes
  • Adding the route to the wrong route table
  • Not associating the correct subnets with the route table
  • Forgetting to add all needed on-premises CIDR blocks
Analogy: static routes are like manually writing directions on a map. They work until the road network changes and you must edit the map yourself.

screens.title: Route propagation and BGP
screens.narratorSegment: Route propagation uses BGP advertisements from your Customer Gateway to populate VPC route tables automatically. When you enable propagation for a VGW on a route table, prefixes that your on-premises device advertises over BGP appear as route entries with VGW as the target. This is especially useful for environments with multiple on-premises subnets or when you want automatic failover: if a tunnel goes down the BGP advertisement is withdrawn and the route disappears, preventing traffic from being sent into a dead path. A concrete example: your CGW advertises 10.0.0.0/16 and 10.1.0.0/24; once propagation is enabled those two routes appear in the VPC route table and traffic to either range follows the VGW. Be careful: enabling propagation does not alter your on-premises routing—your on-prem router still needs to learn the VPC CIDR. A common misconception is assuming route propagation removes the need to verify route origins; you should still confirm which prefixes were learned and that BGP sessions are established. Operational steps include enabling route propagation from the Route Tables console or with aws ec2 enable-vpn-gateway-route-propagation. The takeaway: propagation reduces manual errors and supports resilient routing when BGP is healthy.

keyIdea.title: Propagation benefit
keyIdea.text: Route propagation automates VPC route population using BGP, enabling dynamic discovery and failover of on-prem prefixes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Route Propagation & BGP
How it works
When BGP is established between your on-premises device and the VGW, the CGW advertises prefixes and the VGW learns them. Enabling route propagation on a VPC route table copies those learned prefixes into the table with the VGW as the target.
Enable propagation (CLI)
aws ec2 enable-vpn-gateway-route-propagation \
  --route-table-id rtb-0fedcba9876543210 \
  --vpn-gateway-id vgw-0abcdef1234567890
Benefits & cautions
  • Automates route updates and reduces manual errors
  • Provides automatic failover when BGP withdraws prefixes
  • Requires BGP sessions to be established and healthy
Misconception: propagation does not replace verifying on-prem advertisements. You must confirm the CGW advertises the expected CIDRs.
Key Takeaway

Use propagation to simplify management and enable dynamic reachability, but always validate BGP advertisements and session state.

screens.title: On-premises routing for VPNs
screens.narratorSegment: On the on-premises side, your router or firewall must have routes to reach the VPC CIDR blocks. With static routing you add a route that points the VPC CIDR to the inside tunnel IP address provided in the VPN tunnel details. For example, if your VPC is 172.31.0.0/16, you would configure a static route: Destination 172.31.0.0/16, Next Hop = the tunnel inside IP for the corresponding tunnel. Many setups configure two routes—one per tunnel—with different administrative distances to prefer a primary tunnel. With BGP you peer from your on-prem device to the VGW and your device will learn the VPC CIDR automatically; the VGW will advertise the VPC prefixes to your router. A practical pitfall is forgetting to advertise your on-prem CIDRs to the VGW when using BGP—this means AWS will not learn how to reach your networks. Another misconception is assuming on-prem devices will automatically prefer AWS-learned prefixes; you must inspect administrative distance or local policies. In summary, ensure your on-prem routing either statically maps VPC CIDRs to tunnel inside addresses or uses BGP peering that exchanges CIDRs in both directions. A short check: run show ip route or equivalent and confirm the VPC prefixes are present and point to the tunnel or to the BGP-learned path.

keyIdea.title: On-prem routing rule
keyIdea.text: Configure static next hops to tunnel inside IPs or establish BGP peering so on-prem devices learn VPC prefixes automatically.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › On-prem Routing
On-prem configuration patterns
Static route: destination equals 172.31.0.0/16 and next hop equals the inside tunnel IP reported by AWS. Dynamic: establish BGP peering with the VGW so your device learns 172.31.0.0/16 automatically.
Static route example
Destination: 172.31.0.0/16 Next Hop: tunnel inside IP for tunnel 1
BGP peer example
Establish BGP session to the VGW tunnel IPs and ensure your device advertises local CIDRs to AWS.
Tip: when using static routes, configure both tunnels with different administrative distances or metrics so failover is predictable.
Checks
  • show ip route — look for 172.31.0.0/16
  • show ip bgp summary — ensure BGP is Established
  • Verify advertised prefixes include your on-prem CIDRs
Key Takeaway

On-prem and AWS routing must be symmetrical: both sides need explicit knowledge of remote CIDRs and valid next hops.

screens.title: Static routes vs. Route propagation (BGP)
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between static routes and route propagation depends on your environment and operational preferences. Static routes give you absolute control: you explicitly list each on-premises CIDR in the VPC route table with the VGW as a target. This is simple for small, stable networks and when you cannot run BGP. However, static configuration is error-prone at scale because every change on the on-premises side must be reflected manually in AWS. Route propagation, backed by BGP, reduces manual work and supports automatic failover: if a path goes down BGP withdraws the prefix and AWS stops sending traffic that way. A concrete example in the chapter describes a CGW advertising 10.0.0.0/16 and 10.1.0.0/24; enabling propagation copies both into the VPC route table automatically. A common misconception is thinking BGP removes all operational work; in reality you must still validate advertised prefixes, BGP state, and ensure no overlapping CIDRs exist. Operational trade-offs: use static routes for simple, controlled environments or in cases where your on-premises device cannot peer BGP; use propagation for dynamic, multi-prefix networks or when you want automatic prefix withdrawal. Final question: which approach will scale better for dozens of on-premises subnets?

keyIdea.title: Comparison summary
keyIdea.text: Static routes are manual and predictable; propagation automates prefix distribution and supports failover via BGP.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Static vs Propagation
Static Routes
  • Manual entries per on-prem CIDR
  • Useful when BGP is unavailable
  • Risk of human error at scale
Example: Add 10.0.0.0/16 → vgw-0abcdef1234567890 via create-route.
Route Propagation (BGP)
  • Automatically learns prefixes via BGP
  • Supports automatic withdrawal on failure
  • Requires established BGP sessions
Example: CGW advertises 10.0.0.0/16 and 10.1.0.0/24; enable propagation to import these prefixes.
Decision Tip
If you expect many on-prem prefixes or automatic failover, prefer BGP propagation. If you have a small static footprint or cannot run BGP, use static routes but maintain good audit controls.

screens.title: CLI examples and verification commands
screens.narratorSegment: This screen walks through the exact AWS CLI commands referenced in the chapter so you can perform configuration and verification. To add a static route you run aws ec2 create-route with the route table id, destination CIDR and vpn-gateway-id. To enable propagation for a VGW run aws ec2 enable-vpn-gateway-route-propagation with the route-table-id and vpn-gateway-id. To view routes run describe-route-tables and inspect the RouteTables[]. Routes[] output for a DestinationCidrBlock field matching your on-prem CIDR and a GatewayId matching your VGW. A practical CLI sequence: enable propagation on the main route table rtb-0fedcba9876543210 for vgw-0abcdef1234567890, then describe the route table and look for 10.0.0.0/16 with origin 'propagated'. Remember to also modify security groups, for example to allow ICMP from 10.0.0.0/16 into sg-0123456789abcdef0 using authorize-security-group-ingress. A common misconception is to run commands without verifying associations; always confirm the route table you updated is actually associated with the subnets hosting EC2 instances you will test. Final takeaway: the CLI gives reproducible commands but always follow with describe and a live ping test to validate connectivity. CLI examples and verification commands means use create-route, enable-vpn-gateway-route-propagation, and describe-route-tables, then test with ping and security group checks.. In practical terms, add routes, enable propagation, and inspect route tables with the aws cli. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Routes[] output for a DestinationCidrBlock field matching your on-prem CIDR and a GatewayId matching your VGW. A practical CLI sequence: enable propagation on the main route table rtb-0fedcba9876543210 for vgw-0abcdef1234567890, then describe the route table and look for 10.0.0.0/16 with origin 'propagated'. Remember to also modify security groups, for example to allow ICMP from 10.0.0.0/16 into sg-0123456789abcdef0 using authorize-security-group-ingress. A common misconception is to run commands without verifying associations; always confirm the route table you updated is actually associated with the subnets hosting EC2 instances you will test. Final takeaway: the CLI gives reproducible commands but always follow with describe and a live ping test to validate connectivity. Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › CLI Walkthrough
Commands
# 1. Add a static route for on-prem network
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id rtb-0fedcba9876543210 \
  --destination-cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16 \
  --vpn-gateway-id vgw-0abcdef1234567890

# 2. Enable route propagation for the VGW on a route table
aws ec2 enable-vpn-gateway-route-propagation \
  --route-table-id rtb-0fedcba9876543210 \
  --vpn-gateway-id vgw-0abcdef1234567890

# 3. View routes in a route table
aws ec2 describe-route-tables --route-table-ids rtb-0fedcba9876543210 --query 'RouteTables[].Routes[]'

# 4. Allow inbound ICMP from on-prem 10.0.0.0/16 to EC2 SG
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-0123456789abcdef0 --protocol icmp --port -1 --cidr 10.0.0.0/16
After running these commands, always use describe-route-tables and a live ping from an EC2 instance to an on-prem host to confirm end-to-end reachability.
Verification tips
  • Look for DestinationCidrBlock '10.0.0.0/16' in describe output
  • Check for origin 'propagated' to confirm BGP learned it
  • Run a ping from EC2 to on-prem and check return path
Key Takeaway

CLI commands are reproducible; pair them with describe commands and pings to validate success.

screens.title: Common routing mistakes and how to spot them
screens.narratorSegment: When traffic fails across a Site-to-Site VPN the root cause is usually one of a small set of issues. The most frequent error is missing or incorrect routes: either the VPC route table lacks the on-prem CIDR, or the on-prem device lacks the VPC CIDR. The second frequent area is firewall rules: security groups on EC2 or on-premises firewalls can silently drop ICMP or application traffic even though the tunnel and routes are present. Third, route table association errors occur when you add a route to a route table that is not associated with the subnets hosting your instances. Fourth, source/destination checks on EC2 instances configured as routers can block traffic if not disabled. Fifth, overlapping CIDRs between VPC and on-prem networks create ambiguity and unpredictable routing — avoid them entirely. Sixth, asymmetric routing can confuse some on-prem devices; BGP mitigates this by giving consistent path selection. Finally, BGP state issues prevent route exchange; check that sessions are Established and that expected prefixes are advertised. Practical troubleshooting starts with ping tests, then verifying tunnel status in the AWS console, checking route tables and associations, confirming security groups and NACLs, and inspecting BGP session state. The takeaway: follow a methodical checklist to narrow the problem quickly rather than changing many settings at once.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Common Mistakes
Checklist
  1. Ping test from EC2 to on-prem and reverse
  2. Verify tunnels are UP in the AWS console
  3. Confirm routes exist in VPC route table and on-prem routing
  4. Check security groups and NACLs for allowed traffic
  5. Inspect BGP state and advertised prefixes
Example command to inspect BGP state (on the device): show ip bgp summary. In AWS console check the VPN connection tunnel details for BGP Status.
Common root causes

  • Route added to wrong route table or wrong association
  • Security groups blocking the traffic

Work down the checklist methodically: verify path, then routing, then firewall, then BGP, so you isolate the exact failure point.

screens.title: Activity: Enable route propagation and verify
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks you through enabling route propagation for a VGW and verifying the on-premises route appears in the VPC route table. Use the sample environment: VPC vpc-0123456789abcdef0, VGW vgw-0abcdef1234567890, main route table rtb-0fedcba9876543210, and on-premises CIDR 10.0.0.0/16. Step one: enable propagation with aws ec2 enable-vpn-gateway-route-propagation using the route table and VGW id. Step two: run aws ec2 describe-route-tables to list routes and look for DestinationCidrBlock 10.0.0.0/16 with an origin indicating it was propagated. Step three: from an EC2 instance in a subnet associated with that route table, ping an on-premises host to validate reachability. If ping fails, consult the checklist: are the tunnels up, is the EC2 security group allowing ICMP from 10.0.0.0/16, and is the on-prem device advertising its prefixes? Example CLI commands are provided on the screen for you to copy and adapt. A frequent misconception is trusting the console alone; always pair console checks with live tests from instances because only then can you confirm end-to-end reachability. Finish by disabling propagation only if you have a compelling operational reason; otherwise propagation is safe for dynamic environments.

Task
Enable route propagation for the VGW on the main route table, then verify the 10.0.0.0/16 route appears and test connectivity from an EC2 instance.
# Enable Route Propagation
aws ec2 enable-vpn-gateway-route-propagation \
  --route-table-id rtb-0fedcba9876543210 \

Verification & troubleshooting
  • Confirm describe-route-tables shows 10.0.0.0/16 with origin 'propagated'
  • Ping from an EC2 instance to on-prem and check for replies
  • If ping fails: check tunnel status, security groups, route associations, BGP state and on-prem advertisements
Reflection: after enabling propagation, did the route appear immediately? If not, check BGP session state and that your CGW is actually advertising the prefix.

screens.title: Verifying BGP and tunnel state
screens.narratorSegment: When you rely on BGP and route propagation, verifying BGP state is essential. The VGW and Customer Gateway must establish BGP sessions so prefixes can be learned and propagated. On the on-premises device look for the BGP session to be Established using commands like show ip bgp summary; in the AWS console check the VPN connection Tunnel Details for BGP Status. Next, confirm which prefixes are being advertised by the CGW and which prefixes the VGW advertises back. In AWS you see propagated routes in the route table and can identify their origin in the Routes list. A concrete example: if the CGW advertises 10.0.0.0/16 and the VGW shows that prefix in the VPC route table, propagation is working. A common misconception is to assume an Established BGP session implies correct prefix exchange; the session may be up but not advertising the expected networks, or prefix filters could be applied on the on-prem device. If you see missing routes while BGP is Established, check the on-prem advertisement configuration. Closing question: if the route is not present but BGP is Established, which device should you inspect first for advertisement misconfiguration?

Checks to perform
  • Confirm tunnel status is UP in the AWS console

If BGP is Established but routes are missing, inspect on-prem advertisement configuration and any prefix filters. Also check that propagation is enabled on the right route table.
Quick reference

On-prem: show ip route and show ip bgp summary to ensure VPC prefixes are present and BGP peers are exchanging routes.

Always validate both tunnel health and BGP advertisements; both are required for propagation to work.

screens.title: Example scenario: diagnosing one-way connectivity
screens.narratorSegment: Consider a concrete scenario: on-prem hosts can reach EC2 instances, but EC2 cannot reach on-premises servers. The VPN tunnels show UP in the console. To diagnose, follow a methodical sequence. First, from EC2 run a ping to an on-prem host and capture the failure. Second, examine the EC2 instance's security group and NACLs to confirm outbound traffic for the destination and inbound responses are allowed from 10.0.0.0/16. Third, inspect the VPC route table associated with that subnet; check for a route to 10.0.0.0/16 and verify its target is the VGW. If using BGP, check that route propagation is enabled and that the route appears as propagated; if static, verify the manual entry exists. Fourth, on the on-prem device, run show ip route to ensure the VPC CIDR 172.31.0.0/16 is present and points to the tunnel. Fifth, confirm BGP sessions are Established and prefixes are advertised. A common root cause in this example is that route propagation was not enabled for the VGW, causing AWS to lack a route back to on-prem even though the on-prem device can reach AWS. Closing thought: always pair console checks with live tests to isolate one-way issues quickly.

fullNarratorScript:
Routing is the backbone of any hybrid cloud link. In this chapter you will learn how AWS VPC route tables and your on-premises router cooperate so that EC2 instances and on-premises hosts can communicate over a Site-to-Site VPN. We’ll explain the Virtual Private Gateway’s role as a next hop, contrast static routes with dynamic route propagation using BGP, and show the checks you must run when traffic fails. You will see concrete examples using the sample VPC CIDR 172.31.0.0/16, an on-premises CIDR 10.0.0.0/16 and a VGW ID, and we’ll walk through the AWS CLI commands you can use to add a static route or enable route propagation. You’ll also learn common troubleshooting items: missing routes, incorrect route table associations, security group and firewall rules, overlapping CIDRs, source/destination checks, and BGP session state problems. By the end of this lesson you will be able to decide when to use static routing versus BGP propagation, apply the correct route entries or propagation settings, and verify that routes appear and are functioning. Think about a time you’ve seen one-way connectivity. This chapter will help you find whether the cause is routing, firewalls, or a BGP mismatch.

These objectives focus your attention on the practical routing skills needed for a Site-to-Site VPN. First, you will understand how routing behaves in a hybrid cloud setup so you can reason about packet flow and next hops. Second, you will be able to configure VPC route tables to direct traffic toward your Virtual Private Gateway, using either static routes or automated propagation. Third, you will learn to interpret BGP advertisements from the Customer Gateway so you can verify which prefixes are visible to AWS. Finally, you will acquire troubleshooting techniques: checking routes on both sides, verifying security groups and firewalls, and diagnosing common misconfigurations like overlapping CIDRs. Each objective is framed with examples and a short mnemonic to help retention. For instance, think of route propagation as an automatic mail carrier that delivers addresses learned from BGP into your VPC route book. Practically, you’ll run AWS CLI commands to enable propagation and to add static routes, and you’ll practice verifying the resulting entries. The goal is not only to know the steps but to reason about why a route is missing or why traffic is blocked. This chapter rewards careful verification of both routing tables and firewall rules so the network works end-to-end.

This second objectives slide focuses on the hands-on skills and verification steps. You will enable or add routes using the AWS CLI and confirm that route entries are present. For example, you will run a command to create a static route that points 10.0.0.0/16 to your VGW, or run the route propagation enable command for a given route table. You will also learn how to configure on-premises devices: for static routing add a route to the VPC CIDR with the tunnel inside IP as next-hop, or for BGP peerings verify that your on-premises device advertises local CIDRs and receives the VPC CIDRs. The objective includes performing end-to-end tests: ping from an EC2 instance to an on-prem host and confirm return traffic. You will learn how to interpret commands like show ip route and show ip bgp summary on your device, and how to read the Routes tab in the AWS console. Finally, you will practice a short troubleshooting flow: check tunnel status, check security groups and NACLs, confirm route table entries and associations, and verify BGP sessions. These verifications will build confidence that routing, not a firewall or CIDR overlap, is the root cause of connectivity problems.

In a hybrid cloud setup, routing is the set of rules that tell a host where to send packets when the destination is outside its local subnet. On AWS, each subnet points to a route table that lists destination CIDR blocks and the next hop for matching traffic. For Site-to-Site VPNs the next hop is commonly the Virtual Private Gateway. On-premises routers have matching rules that send packets toward the tunnel or a specific inside-tunnel address. The key claim is this: packets only travel where both sides have explicit knowledge of the remote CIDR and a valid next hop. A concrete example from this chapter uses a VPC CIDR of 172.31.0.0/16 and an on-premises CIDR of 10.0.0.0/16. If an EC2 instance with private IP 172.31.10.5 wants to reach 10.0.2.20, its subnet route table must contain a route for 10.0.0.0/16 pointing to the VGW so the packet is forwarded into the tunnel. A common misconception is believing that an active VPN tunnel alone guarantees connectivity. Tunnels only carry packets when the routing tables on both ends direct traffic toward them. The takeaway: always verify both AWS route tables and on-premises routing entries whenever reachability fails. Which side will you check first when you see a failed ping?

Static routing means you add explicit entries in your VPC route table for each on-premises CIDR and set the target to the Virtual Private Gateway. This process is necessary when you selected static routing at VPN creation or when you need full control over exact prefixes. For example, use the destination 10.0.0.0/16 and set the target to vgw-0abcdef1234567890 so any instance with matching traffic sends packets to the VGW. Important operational advice: every subnet uses an associated route table, so ensure you add the static route to the route table associated with the subnets that require access to on-premises resources. A common mistake is adding a route to the wrong route table or forgetting an association. Another misstep is assuming a single route table is global across the VPC — it is not; associations determine which subnets inherit those routes. The procedural steps are straightforward: open the VPC console, pick the correct route table, and create a route with the on-premises destination and the VGW target. If you use the CLI, run aws ec2 create-route with route-table-id, destination-cidr-block and vpn-gateway-id. Always verify after creation by listing routes and testing connectivity. Closing takeaway: static routes are simple but brittle; they are best for stable, predictable address plans.

Route propagation uses BGP advertisements from your Customer Gateway to populate VPC route tables automatically. When you enable propagation for a VGW on a route table, prefixes that your on-premises device advertises over BGP appear as route entries with VGW as the target. This is especially useful for environments with multiple on-premises subnets or when you want automatic failover: if a tunnel goes down the BGP advertisement is withdrawn and the route disappears, preventing traffic from being sent into a dead path. A concrete example: your CGW advertises 10.0.0.0/16 and 10.1.0.0/24; once propagation is enabled those two routes appear in the VPC route table and traffic to either range follows the VGW. Be careful: enabling propagation does not alter your on-premises routing—your on-prem router still needs to learn the VPC CIDR. A common misconception is assuming route propagation removes the need to verify route origins; you should still confirm which prefixes were learned and that BGP sessions are established. Operational steps include enabling route propagation from the Route Tables console or with aws ec2 enable-vpn-gateway-route-propagation. The takeaway: propagation reduces manual errors and supports resilient routing when BGP is healthy.

On the on-premises side, your router or firewall must have routes to reach the VPC CIDR blocks. With static routing you add a route that points the VPC CIDR to the inside tunnel IP address provided in the VPN tunnel details. For example, if your VPC is 172.31.0.0/16, you would configure a static route: Destination 172.31.0.0/16, Next Hop = the tunnel inside IP for the corresponding tunnel. Many setups configure two routes—one per tunnel—with different administrative distances to prefer a primary tunnel. With BGP you peer from your on-prem device to the VGW and your device will learn the VPC CIDR automatically; the VGW will advertise the VPC prefixes to your router. A practical pitfall is forgetting to advertise your on-prem CIDRs to the VGW when using BGP—this means AWS will not learn how to reach your networks. Another misconception is assuming on-prem devices will automatically prefer AWS-learned prefixes; you must inspect administrative distance or local policies. In summary, ensure your on-prem routing either statically maps VPC CIDRs to tunnel inside addresses or uses BGP peering that exchanges CIDRs in both directions. A short check: run show ip route or equivalent and confirm the VPC prefixes are present and point to the tunnel or to the BGP-learned path.

Choosing between static routes and route propagation depends on your environment and operational preferences. Static routes give you absolute control: you explicitly list each on-premises CIDR in the VPC route table with the VGW as a target. This is simple for small, stable networks and when you cannot run BGP. However, static configuration is error-prone at scale because every change on the on-premises side must be reflected manually in AWS. Route propagation, backed by BGP, reduces manual work and supports automatic failover: if a path goes down BGP withdraws the prefix and AWS stops sending traffic that way. A concrete example in the chapter describes a CGW advertising 10.0.0.0/16 and 10.1.0.0/24; enabling propagation copies both into the VPC route table automatically. A common misconception is thinking BGP removes all operational work; in reality you must still validate advertised prefixes, BGP state, and ensure no overlapping CIDRs exist. Operational trade-offs: use static routes for simple, controlled environments or in cases where your on-premises device cannot peer BGP; use propagation for dynamic, multi-prefix networks or when you want automatic prefix withdrawal. Final question: which approach will scale better for dozens of on-premises subnets?

When traffic fails across a Site-to-Site VPN the root cause is usually one of a small set of issues. The most frequent error is missing or incorrect routes: either the VPC route table lacks the on-prem CIDR, or the on-prem device lacks the VPC CIDR. The second frequent area is firewall rules: security groups on EC2 or on-premises firewalls can silently drop ICMP or application traffic even though the tunnel and routes are present. Third, route table association errors occur when you add a route to a route table that is not associated with the subnets hosting your instances. Fourth, source/destination checks on EC2 instances configured as routers can block traffic if not disabled. Fifth, overlapping CIDRs between VPC and on-prem networks create ambiguity and unpredictable routing — avoid them entirely. Sixth, asymmetric routing can confuse some on-prem devices; BGP mitigates this by giving consistent path selection. Finally, BGP state issues prevent route exchange; check that sessions are Established and that expected prefixes are advertised. Practical troubleshooting starts with ping tests, then verifying tunnel status in the AWS console, checking route tables and associations, confirming security groups and NACLs, and inspecting BGP session state. The takeaway: follow a methodical checklist to narrow the problem quickly rather than changing many settings at once.

This hands-on activity walks you through enabling route propagation for a VGW and verifying the on-premises route appears in the VPC route table. Use the sample environment: VPC vpc-0123456789abcdef0, VGW vgw-0abcdef1234567890, main route table rtb-0fedcba9876543210, and on-premises CIDR 10.0.0.0/16. Step one: enable propagation with aws ec2 enable-vpn-gateway-route-propagation using the route table and VGW id. Step two: run aws ec2 describe-route-tables to list routes and look for DestinationCidrBlock 10.0.0.0/16 with an origin indicating it was propagated. Step three: from an EC2 instance in a subnet associated with that route table, ping an on-premises host to validate reachability. If ping fails, consult the checklist: are the tunnels up, is the EC2 security group allowing ICMP from 10.0.0.0/16, and is the on-prem device advertising its prefixes? Example CLI commands are provided on the screen for you to copy and adapt. A frequent misconception is trusting the console alone; always pair console checks with live tests from instances because only then can you confirm end-to-end reachability. Finish by disabling propagation only if you have a compelling operational reason; otherwise propagation is safe for dynamic environments.

When you rely on BGP and route propagation, verifying BGP state is essential. The VGW and Customer Gateway must establish BGP sessions so prefixes can be learned and propagated. On the on-premises device look for the BGP session to be Established using commands like show ip bgp summary; in the AWS console check the VPN connection Tunnel Details for BGP Status. Next, confirm which prefixes are being advertised by the CGW and which prefixes the VGW advertises back. In AWS you see propagated routes in the route table and can identify their origin in the Routes list. A concrete example: if the CGW advertises 10.0.0.0/16 and the VGW shows that prefix in the VPC route table, propagation is working. A common misconception is to assume an Established BGP session implies correct prefix exchange; the session may be up but not advertising the expected networks, or prefix filters could be applied on the on-prem device. If you see missing routes while BGP is Established, check the on-prem advertisement configuration. Closing question: if the route is not present but BGP is Established, which device should you inspect first for advertisement misconfiguration?

Consider a concrete scenario: on-prem hosts can reach EC2 instances, but EC2 cannot reach on-premises servers. The VPN tunnels show UP in the console. To diagnose, follow a methodical sequence. First, from EC2 run a ping to an on-prem host and capture the failure. Second, examine the EC2 instance's security group and NACLs to confirm outbound traffic for the destination and inbound responses are allowed from 10.0.0.0/16. Third, inspect the VPC route table associated with that subnet; check for a route to 10.0.0.0/16 and verify its target is the VGW. If using BGP, check that route propagation is enabled and that the route appears as propagated; if static, verify the manual entry exists. Fourth, on the on-prem device, run show ip route to ensure the VPC CIDR 172.31.0.0/16 is present and points to the tunnel. Fifth, confirm BGP sessions are Established and prefixes are advertised. A common root cause in this example is that route propagation was not enabled for the VGW, causing AWS to lack a route back to on-prem even though the on-prem device can reach AWS. Closing thought: always pair console checks with live tests to isolate one-way issues quickly.

These three compact cards summarize the essentials you should carry forward. First: VPC route tables define next hops for subnet traffic; to reach on-prem you must point relevant destination CIDRs to the VGW. Second: static routes require manual entries and correct route table associations; route propagation with BGP automates prefix distribution and supports failover. Third: troubleshooting requires checking routes on both sides, validating security groups and firewalls, verifying BGP session state, and ensuring no overlapping CIDRs exist. Keep these checkpoints in mind when designing and validating hybrid connectivity so you focus on the likely causes of failure and avoid common misconfigurations. Keep these final reminders in mind as you configure Site-to-Site VPN routing. First, always ensure your route tables point on-premises CIDRs to the VGW so EC2 traffic knows the next hop. Second, prefer BGP propagation when you need dynamic prefix exchange and automatic failover, but verify the CGW advertises the expected prefixes. Third, never forget to check security groups, NACLs and on-prem firewalls — routes without matching firewall rules will still block traffic.
